nodes.name: Replay webhook
nodes.notes:
POST {"id": 42}. This is the endpoint that makes the dead letter a queue instead of a graveyard: once the cause is fixed, recovering the work is a request, not somebody writing UPDATE statements against production at midnight.

Authentication is a Header Auth credential, assigned in the UI after import. An n8n webhook URL is public the moment the workflow is active, and this one re-runs work that sends email. The token is a credential rather than a config row on purpose: it authenticates a caller rather than configuring behaviour, so it belongs where n8n encrypts it with the instance key and no Code node can read it. n8n also compares it in the framework rather than in an expression, which is one fewer place to get a string comparison subtly wrong.

nodes.name: Replay the oldest by hand
nodes.notes: The editor entry point, for when you are looking at the dead letter list and want to try one.

parameters.query:
SELECT id
FROM dead_letters
WHERE replayed_at IS NULL
  AND reason <> 'invalid'
ORDER BY created_at
LIMIT 1;

nodes.name: Oldest open dead letter
nodes.notes: reason 'invalid' is excluded. A malformed payload will be exactly as malformed on a replay, so offering it up is offering a guaranteed second failure. Those need the source fixed, not the work re-run.

parameters.query:
-- The claim, and the whole reason a replay is safe.
--
-- WHERE replayed_at IS NULL inside the UPDATE is the lock. Two operators
-- clicking replay on the same row at the same second produce one UPDATE that
-- matches and one that matches nothing -- the database decides, not a
-- check-then-act sequence in the workflow that has a gap between the check
-- and the act. Without it, a nervous operator pressing the button three
-- times pays somebody three times.
--
-- The outer SELECT always returns exactly one row, so the next node can read
-- `claimed` and branch. A bare UPDATE ... RETURNING returns nothing when it
-- matches nothing, and a node with no output items looks identical to a node
-- that was never reached.
WITH claimed AS (
  UPDATE dead_letters
  SET replayed_at = now(), replay_execution_id = $2
  WHERE id = $1 AND replayed_at IS NULL
  RETURNING id, kind, payload, error
)
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM claimed)::int AS claimed,
       (SELECT kind    FROM claimed) AS kind,
       (SELECT payload FROM claimed) AS payload,
       (SELECT error   FROM claimed) AS original_error,
       $1::bigint AS dead_letter_id;

nodes.name: Replayable kind?
nodes.notes: 'payout' is deliberately not replayable from here. A held payout is not work that failed, it is a number a human has to agree with, and re-running the computation produces the same number. Wiring it up anyway would turn a deliberate stop into a button somebody presses to make the alert go away.

nodes.name: Back into the pipeline
nodes.notes:
Enters 01 through its single entry point, the same one the poller uses, so one applicant is reprocessed rather than a whole poll. Nothing downstream can tell this apart from a scheduled run.

waitForSubWorkflow is true here, unlike in the poller: a replay is a deliberate act by a person who is waiting to hear whether it worked, and a replay that fails again has to come back here to release its claim.

parameters.query:
INSERT INTO runs
  (workflow_id, execution_id, kind, status, item_count, duration_ms)
VALUES ($1, $2, 'replay', 'ok', 1,
        $3);

-- The replay failed too. Release the claim so the row is open again, and
-- record why on the original dead letter rather than creating a second one:
-- one piece of failed work is one row, however many times it has been tried.
UPDATE dead_letters
SET replayed_at = NULL,
    replay_execution_id = NULL,
    attempts = attempts + 1,
    error = $2
WHERE id = $1
RETURNING id, attempts;

nodes.name: Release the claim
nodes.notes: Without this a failed replay leaves the row marked replayed, and the work is lost with a timestamp saying it was handled. That is worse than never having replayed it, because now nothing is counting it.

assignments.name: message
assignments.value: =Dead letter {{ $json.dead_letter_id }} was already replayed, or does not exist. Nothing was re-run.

nodes.name: Already replayed
nodes.notes: Refused, and says so plainly. A replay endpoint that silently does nothing on a double click teaches the operator that the button does not work, and the next thing they try is the database.

assignments.name: message
assignments.value: =Dead letter {{ $json.dead_letter_id }} is of kind '{{ $json.kind }}' and needs a person, not a re-run.

parameters.query:
-- The claim is taken before the kind is known, because the kind is a column
-- of the row being claimed. So a dead letter that turns out to need a person
-- has to be put back, or it sits there marked replayed, having never been
-- replayed, and drops out of every count that matters.
--
-- attempts is NOT incremented here. Nothing was attempted.
UPDATE dead_letters
SET replayed_at = NULL, replay_execution_id = NULL
WHERE id = $1
RETURNING id;

nodes.name: Replay from the dashboard
nodes.notes: The 'Reintentar' button in 07. Enters at the claim, so a replay from the dashboard goes through exactly the same atomic UPDATE as one from the webhook: two clicks produce one replay and one 'already replayed', decided by the database.
